<reason>Both sides built coherent, well-supported cases and answered pressure questions in proper A1/A2 format, but B's rebuttals did more structural damage. B's epistemic critique of Oregon's self-reported "no coercion" data undercut A's key empirical anchor rather than merely asserting a counter-fact. B's "laundering" argument (family pressure gets certified as free choice through a two-visit process) directly answered A's "legalization adds witnesses" claim rather than just restating it, and A's reply (A4.4) never fully rebutted the mechanism, only reasserted the counterfactual. B also sustained the killing/letting-die and doctrine-of-double-effect distinction through B2.5, while A engaged it once (A2.5) and then dropped it for the rest of the debate, effectively conceding the point on the table. Most importantly, B's case attacks the actual wording of the motion ("under strict safeguards") by arguing such safeguards are structurally unstable once the underlying principle is conceded — a sharper, more resolution-focused framing than A's population-of-one ALS example, which is vivid but was met with a substantive (if unwelcome) answer (continued right to refuse treatment/palliative sedation) that A's closing characterized rhetorically rather than dismantled. A's Oregon "25 years without expansion" counterexample is a genuine and under-rebutted strength, and A's closing framing of certain vs. speculative harm was clean, which keeps this close — but on balance B's chain of rebuttals landed more cleanly and left fewer live threads for A to exploit.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's mechanism argument that legalization "launders" family/caregiver pressure through a two-visit clinical process into certified "free choice" (B2.4/B4.4), which A never fully neutralized beyond reasserting the unregulated-status-quo comparison.</best_rebuttal>
